description: This case study is a lesson-learned page from ASDSO's Dam Failures and Lessons Learned site on why timely warning and rapid public response decide loss of life in a dam emergency. It defines a dam incident as an impending or actual sudden uncontrolled release or excessive controlled release of water and says dam owners, operators and community emergency managers must work together to protect residents, workers and visitors. A table lists events with limited, ineffective or no warning: Austin Dam, Pennsylvania, 1911, 78 deaths; Canyon Lake, South Dakota, 1972, 238; Malpasset Dam, France, 1959, 421; South Fork Dam, Pennsylvania, 1889, 2,209; and Vajont Dam, Italy, 1953, 2,056. Eyewitness accounts from the Rapid City flood show how warnings were doubted. The page has tabs for description, photos and videos, case studies, best practices and other resources. Coverage: global historic examples, narrative and table, not a dataset. Access: free web page; licence not stated. Caveats: the fatality table mixes causes and gives no method; this record is based on the description tab only. It informs emergency response simulation, with warning-time, mobilisation and evacuation assumptions for dam-break consequence and life-loss models, and relates to the ASDSO and Stanford incident databases in the catalogue.
